newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries calm in London before big week for U.S..
newsitem.headline: Treasuries calm in London before big week for U.S..

text.p: U.S. Treasuries in London were quiet as month and quarter end approached, but could liven up after Monday's economic data and before the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting and payrolls further out, traders said.

"It seems like not much is going on, but we'll get cooking pretty soon," said a Treasuries trader at a U.S. bank in London. "There are lots of numbers coming out so we could see plenty of volatility."
The 30-year benchmark bond was at 98-16 at 0952 GMT, to yield 6.74 percent, up slightly from 98-13 in Tokyo and level with Friday's New York close.
Two-year T-notes nudged up to 99-31 compared with 99-30 in Tokyo and New York, while five-year notes were also up slightly, at 99-21 versus 99-20 in Tokyo and New York.

For Monday, the immediate focus would be the U.S. May personal income and consumption data, due at 1230 GMT, and May new home sales and June Chicago Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) at 1400 GMT, traders said.
The U.S. bank trader said personal income and consumption did not generally move the market very much.
"The Chicago PMI could get the market going. If its a surprisingly weak number the market could get back up to last week's highs, which is about three-quarters of a point higher," he said.
Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London, also said the Chicago PMI would be the most important of the data on Monday.
"We are looking for it to come in a bit stronger. A rise to around 58 compared with the previous 56.8," he said adding that the Philadelphia Fed Index last week had showed surprising strength.
A Reuters consensus of economists forecasts expected the index to come in at 57.5.
"If it comes in strong it could cause a little bit of an upset but people are really on hold until we get the FOMC meeting and Thursday's payrolls out of the way," Chester said.
But the week would be dominated by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday and the June employment report on Thursday.
There will be a market and public holiday in the U.S. on Friday for Independence Day.
"The market is vulnerable to the downside towards the end of the week," Chester said.

"The FOMC meeting will go without too much of a hitch, I don't expect any move on rates. But the market could be lulling itself into a false sense of security and if we get a strong payrolls figure on Thursday then that could cause a bit of a jolt in the market."
September T-bond futures were at 111-20 in automated trade, unchanged from Friday's Chicago settlement.
The September LIFFE T-bond future was at 111-19, down 1/32 from the Chicago close.
